In the most recent American psychiatric manual, DSM-5 (2013), shared psychotic disorder was removed as a standalone diagnosis, with the reasoning that it could be captured under other existing categories. However, the concept itself remains clinically and academically relevant, and the term folie à deux is still very much in active use.
The Two People Involved: Primary and Secondary

In virtually every case, there are two distinct roles.

The Primary Person (the "Inducer")

This is the person who develops the delusion first and independently. They have a genuine psychotic illness — most commonly paranoid schizophrenia or a delusional disorder. Their delusion is intense, elaborate, and unshakeable. They are typically the more dominant personality in the relationship: more forceful, more emotionally controlling, or more persuasive.

The Secondary Person (the "Recipient")

This is the person who adopts the delusion from the primary person. Crucially, before the relationship with the primary person, they were usually mentally healthy. They are often more passive, more dependent, and more suggestible. They are not "mad" on their own; their shared belief is a product of the relationship.

The secondary person genuinely comes to believe the delusion. It's not performance, loyalty, or pretending to keep the peace. Over time, through constant reinforcement and emotional pressure, the delusion becomes real in their mind.
How Does It Happen? The Mechanics

For folie à deux to develop, several conditions typically come together:

1. Prolonged closeness and isolation
The two people live or spend time together intensely, often cut off from the wider world. This isolation is key — it means the outside reality never effectively challenges or corrects the delusional worldview. The primary person's version of reality fills all the available space.

2. A strong emotional bond with a power imbalance
The relationship is usually one of deep emotional dependence. Common pairings include married couples, parent and child, two siblings, or close friends. Crucially, the secondary person looks up to, loves, fears, or relies on the primary person heavily. This creates a psychological vulnerability to adopting the primary's beliefs.

3. The primary person is persuasive and insistent
The primary person's delusional framework is not quiet — it shapes every interaction. They interpret daily events through its lens. Over months or years, through sheer repetition and emotional weight, this worldview seeps into the secondary person's beliefs.

4. A lack of corrective outside contact
If the secondary person had frequent, warm, trusted social connections outside the pair, those external relationships might provide reality-checking. In folie à deux cases, this corrective network is typically absent or has been deliberately severed.
The Most Important Test: What Happens When They're Separated?

This is one of the most clinically fascinating aspects of the phenomenon. In many cases, when the two people are separated, the secondary person's delusion fades on its own.

This is what distinguishes the secondary person from someone with an independent psychotic illness. Their belief was not rooted in their own biology or individual mental breakdown — it was propped up by the relationship. Remove the relationship, remove the constant reinforcement, reconnect them with reality, and the delusion can dissolve within weeks or months without any medication.

The primary person, by contrast, does not recover simply from separation. Their delusion has its own internal roots and requires active psychiatric treatment.
Types: The Different Varieties Psychiatrists Described

Over the years, clinicians refined the original concept into subtypes based on what exactly happens between the two people.

Folie imposée ("imposed madness")
The most common type. The secondary person passively absorbs the delusion. They were mentally healthy before, they adopt the belief through the relationship, and if separated early enough, they recover well. The delusion is "imposed" on them from outside.

Folie communiquée ("communicated madness")
The secondary person initially resists the delusion — they don't just passively receive it. But over a longer period, the primary person's reality eventually "wins." What makes this type particularly interesting is that even after separation, the secondary person may hold onto the delusion. By the time it's "communicated" fully, it has taken genuine root.

Folie simultanée ("simultaneous madness")
Both people independently develop the same or similar delusions at roughly the same time. Unlike the other types, there is no clear direction of transmission. Both people are primary in a sense. This is relatively rare and controversial as a subtype, since it raises the question of whether they truly influenced each other or simply had similar vulnerabilities and experiences.

Folie induite ("induced madness")
This occurs when someone who already has a psychotic illness adopts additional delusions from someone they're living with who also has a psychotic illness. It's less about transmitting madness to a healthy person and more about one set of delusional ideas cross-pollinating with another.
Extensions Beyond Two People

The concept was never strictly limited to pairs. The same dynamic can involve more people:

  • Folie à trois — madness of three
  • Folie à quatre — madness of four
  • Folie à famille — madness of a family
  • Folie à plusieurs — madness of several (a group or crowd)

In all these cases, the same basic mechanics apply: a charismatic or dominant primary individual with a delusional belief system, close and isolated contact, and a group whose members come to share that belief.

This extension is why the concept is relevant to understanding cults. A charismatic cult leader with delusional or paranoid beliefs can, through isolation, emotional manipulation, and constant reinforcement, cause an entire community to sincerely adopt those beliefs. The Heaven's Gate group and the Jonestown massacre are historical examples that scholars have analyzed through this lens.
Who Is at Risk of Becoming the Secondary Person?

Not everyone in close contact with someone delusional will develop folie à deux. Several factors seem to raise the risk:

  • Emotional dependence: The more you need this person — for love, security, identity — the more vulnerable you are to their reality.
  • Social isolation: The fewer outside connections and reality-checks you have, the more your entire sense of what's real can be shaped by one person.
  • Pre-existing passivity or lower self-assertiveness: People who are naturally more passive or who defer to others are more susceptible.
  • Lower premorbid intelligence or education has been cited in some older literature, though this is debated and should be understood in context.
  • Shared stress or trauma: When two people are going through intense experiences together, the bonds deepen and the vulnerability increases.

It is important to note that none of this makes the secondary person weak or foolish. The conditions of folie à deux are extreme — prolonged isolation, intense emotional dependency, daily reinforcement of a distorted reality. Most human minds, under those conditions, can be shaped in ways they otherwise wouldn't be.
Real-World Examples

June and Jennifer Gibbons — "The Silent Twins"

Perhaps the most widely studied human example. These identical twin sisters from Wales became famous for refusing to speak to anyone except each other. They lived in a world almost entirely of their own making. Their case is complex — they had distinct shared beliefs, rituals, and perceptions of reality that were not accessible to or shared by anyone outside their bond. While not a textbook delusional case in the strictest clinical sense, their extreme mutual psychological enmeshment is one of the most cited examples of the folie à deux dynamic in the broader sense.

Ian Brady and Myra Hindley — The Moors Murderers

Brady was the dominant, psychopathic primary figure. Hindley, before meeting him, had no history of violence or criminal behavior. After years under his intense influence and isolation from outside relationships, she participated in the murders of five children in 1960s England. Many analysts have used the folie à deux framework to understand how a person with no independent violent pathology could be so thoroughly absorbed into another person's psychopathology.

Cult leaders and their followers

Jim Jones (Jonestown, 1978) and Marshall Applewhite of Heaven's Gate are studied as examples where the dynamic scaled up. The leader held a coherent, elaborate delusional framework. Through isolation, love-bombing, sleep deprivation, dietary control, and constant ideological reinforcement, entire communities came to share beliefs that — from outside — were clearly disconnected from reality. Over 900 people died at Jonestown. 39 members of Heaven's Gate died by mass suicide believing they would board a spacecraft hidden in the tail of the Hale-Bopp comet.
How Is It Diagnosed?

Diagnosis requires careful clinical assessment. The psychiatrist or psychologist evaluating the case needs to:

  • Establish that both people share an identical or near-identical delusional belief system
  • Confirm that the secondary person did not independently develop the delusion
  • Understand the nature and history of the relationship (closeness, isolation, power dynamics)
  • Rule out independent psychotic disorders in the secondary person
  • Rule out organic causes (brain tumors, substance use, medical conditions that can mimic psychosis)

Diagnosis is complicated by the fact that both people will typically deny there is anything wrong. From inside the shared delusion, everything makes perfect sense.
How Is It Treated?

Treatment generally involves three components:

1. Separation
The single most important intervention, especially for the secondary person. Physical separation from the primary person removes the constant reinforcement and gives the secondary person a chance to reconnect with outside reality. In many cases, especially early ones, this alone leads to significant recovery in the secondary person.

2. Treating the Primary Person
The primary person's underlying psychiatric condition — typically schizophrenia, delusional disorder, or a mood disorder with psychotic features — must be treated with antipsychotic medication, therapy, and psychiatric care. Without treating the root, even if separated, re-exposure risks the cycle starting again.

3. Psychotherapy for the Secondary Person
Even if the delusion fades after separation, the secondary person may need therapy to process what happened. They often struggle with confusion about what was real, shame, grief over the relationship, and the challenge of rebuilding a sense of themselves and their reality.

Prognosis is generally better for the secondary person than for the primary person. The secondary person's condition is, in many cases, fundamentally relational rather than biological — which means addressing the relationship can directly address the illness.
In Popular Culture

The term and concept have entered popular culture in several ways:

  • The 2024 film "Joker: Folie à Deux" used the term in its title, exploring the shared delusion or co-dependent reality between Arthur Fleck (the Joker) and his love interest.
  • The phrase is used loosely in many crime dramas, thrillers, and discussions of toxic relationships to describe any situation where two people reinforce each other's distorted thinking — though it's worth knowing this popular use is sometimes broader and less precise than the clinical definition.
  • It appears frequently in discussions of codependency, cults, radicalization, and echo chambers, as a conceptual lens even when not a strict clinical diagnosis.
The Broader Lesson

Beyond its clinical definition, folie à deux points to something profound about human psychology: reality is, to a significant degree, socially constructed. Our sense of what is true, normal, and real is constantly shaped by the people around us. Most of the time, living in society with many different relationships provides enough corrective feedback to keep us grounded.

But when we are isolated, dependent on one person, and that person holds a distorted version of reality — our minds are far more malleable than we might assume. This is not a sign of stupidity or weakness. It is a feature of how human cognition works. We are deeply social animals, and our sense of reality is deeply social too.

This is why isolation is a weapon — in abusive relationships, in cults, in authoritarian systems. Remove someone from the corrective network of a diverse social world, and the reality offered by whoever remains is the reality that fills the mind.
Summary at a Glance

• What: A shared delusional disorder where one person's delusion is transmitted to another through close contact.
  • Who: A dominant primary person with psychosis, and a dependent secondary person who absorbs the belief.
  • How: Through isolation, emotional dependency, and constant reinforcement over time.
  • Key test: Separate them — the secondary person's delusion often fades; the primary person's does not.
  • Types: Folie imposée, communiquée, simultanée, and induite.
  • Scale: Can extend to three people, families, or entire groups.
  • Treatment: Separation, treating the primary's psychosis, and therapy for the secondary.
  • Deeper meaning: A window into how malleable human reality can be under extreme social influence.
6277:
Folklore is the collection of traditional stories, beliefs, customs, practices, sayings, songs, and art that a community — a group of people who share something in common, like a culture, religion, region, or ethnicity — passes down from one generation to the next. The key word here is traditional, meaning these things have existed within the group for a long time and have been carried forward over time, not invented recently by one person.

Think of it this way: if your grandmother tells you a story her grandmother once told her, teaches you a remedy for a cold that her village always used, or warns you never to whistle at night because it brings bad luck — that is folklore in action.

Folklore is not just one thing. It is an umbrella term that covers several different types of traditional expression.

Stories. This includes myths (stories that explain how the world came to be or why things are the way they are), legends (stories about real or supposedly real people and places, presented as true), fairy tales (imaginative stories involving magical creatures and moral lessons), fables (short stories featuring animals that teach a lesson), and folk tales (general traditional stories passed around a community).

Beliefs and superstitions. Thinking that breaking a mirror brings seven years of bad luck, that a black cat crossing your path is a bad omen, or that placing a horseshoe above a door brings good fortune — all of these are folklore. They are beliefs that a community has held for generations, even if there is no scientific basis for them.

Customs and rituals. The specific way a community celebrates a wedding, mourns a death, marks the change of seasons, or welcomes a newborn child — when these practices are traditional and have been handed down, they are folklore.

Proverbs and sayings. Short, wise expressions like "too many cooks spoil the broth," "a stitch in time saves nine," or "don't count your chickens before they hatch" are folklore. They carry the accumulated practical wisdom of a group, condensed into a memorable phrase.

Songs, music, and dance. Folk songs sung at harvest time, lullabies mothers have sung to children for centuries, and traditional dances performed at festivals are all folklore.

Jokes and riddles. Even humor that circulates within a community — especially the kind that gets retold and slightly changed by each person — is considered folklore.

Crafts and traditional art. Techniques for weaving a particular kind of basket, decorating pottery in a regional style, or building a specific type of structure using ancestral methods also fall under folklore.

Folk medicine. Traditional remedies and healing practices passed down within a community — like using honey and ginger for a sore throat because elders have always done so — are folklore too.

Simply being old or traditional is not enough to call something folklore. There are specific qualities that define it.

It belongs to a community, not an individual. Great novels are written by named authors. Famous paintings are created by known artists. Folklore, however, has no single original creator that anyone can point to. It belongs to the whole group. Nobody invented the legend of King Arthur on a Tuesday afternoon and signed their name to it. It grew, shaped by countless unnamed people across generations.

It is passed down informally. Folklore does not travel through textbooks, formal classrooms, or official institutions. It travels through conversation, observation, imitation, and practice. A child learns a superstition by hearing a parent mention it. A young person learns a traditional dance by watching elders perform it at a festival. This informal, person-to-person transmission is central to what folklore is.

It changes as it travels. Because it is passed down through word of mouth and practice rather than through fixed, written records, folklore naturally shifts and evolves. Each person who retells a story may add a detail, drop another, or change a name. This is why you will find many versions of the same fairy tale across different countries and cultures — each version is a variation that developed as the story moved from one place, person, or time to another. This variation is not a flaw; it is a natural feature of folklore.

It is anonymous. Because of its communal and informal nature, the original creator of most folklore is unknown and unknowable. When you tell someone that knocking on wood prevents bad luck, you have no idea who first thought of that. Neither does anyone else.

It reflects the values, fears, and worldview of its community. Folklore is not random. A culture's folklore reveals what that culture cares about, what it fears, what it finds funny, what it considers moral or immoral, and how it makes sense of the world. Stories about trickster characters who outsmart the powerful reflect communities that admire cleverness. Legends about dangerous forests warn children to stay close to home. Harvest songs reflect communities whose survival depends on agriculture. Folklore is a mirror held up to a culture.
Folklore is not only ancient or rural

A very common mistake people make is thinking folklore belongs only to old, rural, pre-modern societies. This is wrong. Every community — including modern, urban ones — produces and carries folklore.

Urban legends are a perfect example. Stories like "there's an alligator living in the city sewers," or "a man woke up in a bathtub of ice with one kidney missing," or "a fast food restaurant puts addictive chemicals in its food" — these are modern folklore. They are anonymous, they circulate informally (often by word of mouth or through the internet), they vary from telling to telling, and they reflect the anxieties of modern life: distrust of institutions, fear of strangers, vulnerability in cities.

The internet has also created new forms of folklore. Memes that spread and get remixed by thousands of anonymous people, chain messages ("share this or something bad will happen"), and viral rumors are all forms of contemporary digital folklore, because they follow the same pattern: they travel informally, anonymously, within a community, and change as they spread.

Even a school has its own folklore — stories about a supposedly haunted classroom, rumors about a teacher's past, or rituals students perform before an exam. A family has its own folklore too — inside jokes, stories about an ancestor, and traditions nobody quite remembers the origin of.

The academic study of folklore is called folkloristics (or folklore studies). Scholars who do this work are called folklorists. They collect, document, compare, and analyze the folklore of different communities in order to understand human culture, history, and identity. Folklorists do fieldwork — they go into communities, listen to stories, record songs, and interview people — because folklore lives in real human practice, not on a library shelf.

Folklore is not trivial or childish. It is one of the most powerful ways human beings preserve and transmit their identity, values, and understanding of the world.

Before widespread literacy and printing, folklore was essentially how culture survived. History, moral lessons, practical knowledge, and spiritual beliefs were all encoded in stories, songs, and rituals that people could memorize and pass on. Folklore was the hard drive of pre-literate societies.

Even in the modern world, folklore strengthens community bonds. Sharing stories, celebrating traditional festivals, and using the same proverbs creates a sense of belonging and shared identity. It connects the living to those who came before them. It answers the human need to feel part of something larger than oneself.

Folklore also gives historians, anthropologists, and cultural scholars a window into the lives of ordinary people — not kings and rulers, but everyday communities — in ways that official written history often does not. The fears people encoded in their superstitions, the values they embedded in their fairy tales, and the humor they expressed in their jokes tell us things about human experience that no official document ever could.

The word "folklore" is sometimes used loosely in everyday speech to mean a belief or story that is simply false or unscientific — as in, "oh, that's just folklore." This is an inaccurate use of the word. In its proper meaning, folklore is not necessarily false. Some folk remedies are medically effective. Some folk wisdom is genuinely sound. What makes something folklore is how it is transmitted and who it belongs to, not whether it is true or false. A folklorist is interested in the story, belief, or practice as a cultural phenomenon — regardless of its factual accuracy.
6278:
A folktale is a traditional story that originally belonged to the ordinary people of a community — the "folk" — and was passed down from generation to generation by word of mouth, long before anyone wrote it down. Nobody knows who first made up these stories. They have no single author. They grew out of the shared imagination of an entire culture, shaped and reshaped by countless tellers over hundreds or even thousands of years.

Think of it this way: a novel has one author who wrote it on a specific date. A folktale has everyone as its author, and its "publication date" is simply a very long time ago.
What makes a folktale a folktale

Folktales share a set of recognizable qualities that set them apart from other kinds of stories:

1. Anonymous and collective origin
No one person created a folktale. It emerged from a community over time. Even when a scholar like the Brothers Grimm eventually wrote them down, they were simply collecting stories that already existed in oral form among the people.

2. Passed down orally
Before books were common, people sat around fires, in homes, and at festivals and told these stories aloud. A grandmother told her grandchildren, who later told their children, and so on. This oral chain is called the oral tradition. Over time, details change, versions multiply, and the story adapts to fit new places and times — which is why the same folktale often has hundreds of versions across different cultures.

3. Set in a vague, timeless world
Folktales rarely say "this happened in Berlin in the year 1350." Instead they begin with phrases like "Once upon a time…" or "Long ago, in a faraway land…" This deliberate vagueness signals to the listener: this story could have happened anywhere, to anyone, at any time. It is not a news report; it is a truth of a different kind.

4. Simple, archetypal characters
The characters in folktales are not complicated, psychologically layered human beings. They are archetypes — clear, simple roles that stand for universal human types. There is the kind and humble hero, the wicked stepmother, the greedy merchant, the wise old woman in the forest, the clever youngest son. You instantly know who they are and what they represent. This simplicity made the stories easier to remember and retell.

5. Things happen in patterns — especially threes
Folktales love repetition and pattern. Three brothers go on a quest. Three wishes are granted. The hero tries and fails twice, then succeeds on the third attempt. This structure is not accidental — it was a memory tool. Patterns helped storytellers remember and retell the story accurately.

6. A moral or lesson is usually embedded
Most folktales teach something about how to live. Be honest. Don't be greedy. Kindness is rewarded. Pride leads to downfall. The lesson is rarely stated bluntly — it is woven into what happens to the characters. The good are rewarded; the wicked are punished. This made folktales a powerful tool for teaching values to children and reinforcing them in adults.

7. Magic and the supernatural are common
Many folktales — though not all — involve magical elements: enchanted objects, talking animals, witches, fairies, curses, transformations. Magic in folktales is usually a plot device — it creates the obstacle or enables the solution — rather than a system of rules like in modern fantasy fiction.
What folktales do for a society

Folktales are not just entertainment. They serve deep functions:

  • They pass down values. A culture's beliefs about honesty, courage, justice, and humility are baked into its folktales. Children absorb these values through the stories before they are old enough to understand abstract rules.
  • They create shared identity. A community that shares the same stories shares a common world. Knowing the same folktales makes you part of the same people.
  • They process fear and anxiety. Dangers like abandonment, cruelty, death, and the unknown appear in folktales in symbolic form — as witches, wolves, and dark forests. By hearing these stories, people work through their fears in a safe, imaginative space.
  • They explain the world. Some folktales (especially a type called pourquoi tales, meaning "why" tales) explain natural phenomena — why the sky is blue, why the tiger has stripes — in narrative form, before science was available to explain them.
Types of stories that fall under the folktale umbrella

"Folktale" is sometimes used as a broad term that includes several related types of traditional stories. Other times, it is used in a narrow sense to mean one specific type. Here is how the landscape looks:

Fairy tales are folktales with prominent magical and fantastical elements — fairies, spells, magical objects, transformations. Cinderella, Sleeping Beauty, and Rumpelstiltskin are fairy tales. All fairy tales are folktales, but not all folktales are fairy tales.

Fables are very short folktales, often with animal characters, that end with a clearly stated moral lesson. Aesop's stories — the tortoise and the hare, the fox and the crow — are fables.

Trickster tales feature a clever, cunning character (often an animal like a spider, rabbit, or coyote) who outsmarts stronger opponents through wit and guile. These stories often celebrate intelligence over brute strength.

Tall tales are humorous folktales built on wild exaggeration. The hero performs impossible feats on a massive scale. American folk heroes like Paul Bunyan (a giant lumberjack) and Pecos Bill belong to this type.

Pourquoi tales (from the French word for "why") are origin stories that explain why something in nature is the way it is. "How the elephant got its trunk" or "Why the crow is black" are examples.

Myths are sometimes grouped with folktales, but they are somewhat different in character. Myths are sacred stories about gods, the creation of the world, and cosmic events. The people who told them often believed them to be true in a religious sense. Greek stories about Zeus, Norse stories about Odin, and Hindu stories about Brahma creating the universe are myths.

Legends are stories about human heroes or historical events that are believed — or were once believed — to be at least partly true. King Arthur, Robin Hood, and William Tell are legendary figures. Unlike pure folktales, legends are attached to real or semi-real places and times.
Famous examples from around the world

Folktales are not the property of any one culture. Every culture on earth has them:

  • Cinderella (European, but versions exist in almost every culture on earth, including ancient Egypt and China)
  • Anansi the Spider stories (West African and Caribbean) — Anansi is a trickster spider who outsmarts gods and humans alike
  • The Panchatantra stories (Indian) — animal fables teaching wisdom about life and statecraft
  • One Thousand and One Nights / Arabian Nights (Middle Eastern) — including stories like Aladdin and Ali Baba
  • Brer Rabbit stories (African American, rooted in West African trickster traditions)
  • The Ramayana and Mahabharata (Indian) — these sit at the boundary between myth, legend, and folktale
How folktales differ from literary stories

A literary story (a novel, a short story by a named author) is fixed. It was written on a particular day, and it stays that way. A folktale is living and fluid. It changes with each telling. This is why Cinderella has over a thousand documented versions worldwide — each culture adapted it to reflect its own values, landscapes, and concerns. There is no single "correct" version of a folktale. They are all correct, because the story belongs to the people, not to any one text.

A folktale is a traditional, anonymously authored story born from the collective voice of a people, passed down orally across generations, set in a timeless world, featuring simple archetypal characters, and usually carrying a moral or cultural lesson at its heart. It is one of humanity's oldest and most powerful tools for making sense of the world, building community, and passing wisdom from one generation to the next.
6279: Follow means to come after something or someone. But "after" can mean after in place, after in time, after in logic, or after in influence. That is why this one word has so many uses — they all share this single idea of something coming behind, next, or as a result.
1. Moving Behind Someone or Something (Physical Following)

The most basic meaning: you move in the same direction as someone, staying behind them.

  • The child followed her mother through the market.
  • A police car followed the truck for two miles.
  • The dog follows me everywhere I go.

Here, "follow" simply means to go where someone else goes, keeping them ahead of you. It does not mean you are with them or that they know you are there. A shadow follows you. A detective follows a suspect. A crowd follows a leader.
2. Coming After in Time or Order (Sequence)

"Follow" also means to come next in a sequence — after something ends, the next thing follows.

  • Winter follows autumn.
  • A loud explosion followed the flash of light.
  • Please read Chapter 3. Chapter 4 follows.

Notice: the thing that follows always comes second. Whatever you are following always comes first. This is true in all meanings of the word.
3. Going Along a Path or Route

When you follow a road, a river, a sign, or a map, you move along its direction without leaving it.

  • Follow the path until you reach the lake.
  • The road follows the coastline for forty kilometres.
  • Follow the signs to the airport.

Here you are not following a person — you are following a line or a direction. You let the road or path decide where you go.
4. Obeying Instructions, Rules, or Advice

When someone tells you what to do — a rule, an instruction, a recipe, a doctor's order — and you do it, you are following it.

  • Please follow the instructions on the packet.
  • All students must follow the school rules.
  • She followed the doctor's advice and rested for a week.
  • Follow the recipe exactly, or the cake will not rise.

The idea is the same: the instruction came first, your action comes after (behind it). You are letting someone else's words guide your steps.
5. Copying Someone's Example or Doing What They Did

If someone does something before you, and you then do the same thing because of them, you are following their example, their lead, or their footsteps.

  • He followed his grandfather into farming.
  • Many young scientists followed in Marie Curie's footsteps.
  • She set an example, and her teammates followed.
  • The other countries followed France's lead on the new policy.

This meaning is about influence. The person you follow shaped what you do. They came first; you came after, doing similarly.
6. Following a Belief, Philosophy, or Way of Life

You can follow a religion, a philosophy, a diet, or a set of ideas. This means you accept those ideas and live by them.

  • He follows Buddhism.
  • She follows a strict vegetarian diet.
  • Many people in the 1960s followed Gandhi's principles of non-violence.

Again, the structure is the same: those ideas came before you, you accept them, and you align yourself with them.
7. Watching, Tracking, or Keeping Up With Something

To follow news, a sport, a person's career, or a situation means you pay close attention to it regularly. You keep up with what happens.

  • I follow cricket very closely.
  • He has been following the political situation in that country for years.
  • She follows the stock market every single day.
  • Are you following this story? It gets more interesting every day.

Here you are not physically moving. You are keeping your attention on something as it develops over time. You follow each new development as it comes — one after another.
8. Following Someone on Social Media or Online

In modern usage, to follow someone on a platform like Instagram, YouTube, or Twitter means you subscribe to their updates. Their posts appear in your feed automatically.

  • If you like this channel, please follow us.
  • She follows five hundred people on Instagram.
  • I followed him online after seeing his artwork.

This is a technical use, but the idea is the same: they post, you receive it — they are ahead, you are behind, staying updated.
9. Understanding What Someone Is Saying

To follow someone's words or reasoning means to understand them as they speak — to keep up with the flow of what they are saying.

  • Do you follow me? (Do you understand what I am saying?)
  • I couldn't follow the professor's lecture — it was too fast.
  • He explained it simply so that everyone could follow.
  • Sorry, I lost you there. Could you explain that again? I'm not following.

Think of an argument or explanation as a path of ideas. If you follow it, you walk along it successfully. If you lose the thread, you have stopped following.
10. Logical Consequence — "It Follows That…"

In logic and reasoning, if one thing is true and it leads naturally to another conclusion, we say the second follows from the first.

  • If all humans are mortal, and Ravi is human, it follows that Ravi is mortal.
  • She had no ticket and no money. It follows that she could not have taken the train.
  • That doesn't follow — your conclusion doesn't match your evidence.

"It follows that" is a formal way of saying "therefore" or "this is the natural result." The conclusion comes after the evidence, just as things always do when they follow.
11. Pursuing a Career or Passion

To follow a career, a calling, or a dream means to pursue it — to make it the direction of your life.

  • He followed a career in medicine.
  • She finally decided to follow her passion for painting.
  • After years in business, he chose to follow a life of teaching.

The metaphor here is that your dream or career is a path, and you are walking along it.
Summary of All the Ways "Follow" Works

Even though "follow" has many meanings, every single one carries the same underlying logic: something comes first, and the follower comes after or behind it. Whether it is a person walking behind another, a month coming after the last, a student obeying a rule, a reader understanding an argument, or a conclusion arising from evidence — in every case, there is a "first" and a "second," and the second is what follows.
Useful Fixed Expressions With "Follow"

Follow up — to take further action on something already started.
I will follow up with you after the meeting.

Follow through — to complete something you started; to do the full action.
He made a promise but didn't follow through.
In tennis or cricket, "follow through" literally means completing the swing of your arm after you hit.

Follow suit — to do the same as someone else just did (from card games, where you must play the same suit).
One shop dropped its prices and all the others followed suit.

Follow in someone's footsteps — to do the same work, take the same path, or adopt the same lifestyle as someone who came before you.
She followed in her mother's footsteps and became a nurse.

Follow one's heart — to be guided by what you feel deeply, not by logic alone.
He left his well-paid job to follow his heart.

As follows — used to introduce a list or explanation that is coming right after.
The rules are as follows: no phones, no food, no loud talking.

Follow the crowd — to do what everyone else is doing, without thinking independently.
Don't just follow the crowd — make your own decision.

That covers every important meaning and use of the verb "follow." The word is remarkably consistent: it always points to something that comes after, in whatever dimension — space, time, logic, understanding, or influence.
6280:
"Follow suit" means to do the same thing that someone else has done — to copy or imitate someone else's action, often because their action sets an example or creates a kind of pressure for others to do the same.

Think of it this way: Person A does something. Then Person B looks at what Person A did and does the exact same thing (or something very similar). Person B has followed suit.

This idiom comes from card games — specifically games like Bridge, Whist, or similar trick-taking card games that were very popular in earlier centuries.

In these card games, a standard deck has four suits: Hearts, Diamonds, Clubs, and Spades. When one player puts down a card — say, a Heart — the rules require every other player to also play a card from the same suit (Hearts, in this case), if they have one. This rule is called "following suit."

So if the first player leads with a Diamond, you must follow suit — meaning you must also play a Diamond.

Over time, this term left the card table and entered everyday language. People started using it to mean: "do what the first person did." Today, it has absolutely nothing to do with cards — it is a fully general expression used in all kinds of situations.

This is something many learners find confusing, so let's clear it up.

The word "suit" here does not mean a business suit (the clothing). In this idiom, "suit" means a group or category — specifically, the category of the card played. When you follow the suit, you follow the same category or the same type of action.

The idiom is almost always used in this kind of structure:

Someone + followed suit / follows suit / following suit

Notice that "suit" is never changed. You don't say "followed suits" or "followed a suit." It is always "follow suit" (no article, no plural).

Tense Forms:

  • Past: She followed suit.
  • Present: He follows suit.
  • Present Continuous: They are following suit.
  • Infinitive: I decided to follow suit.

Example 1 — Business

"One airline reduced its ticket prices, and all the other airlines quickly followed suit."

What it means: The first airline lowered its prices. The other airlines saw this and did the same thing — they also lowered their prices.

Example 2 — Social Behavior

"My older brother started waking up at 5 AM to exercise every day. Soon, I followed suit."

What it means: The older brother started a new habit. The speaker saw this and began doing the same thing.

Example 3 — Politics / Government

"Germany introduced new environmental laws, and several neighboring countries followed suit."

What it means: Germany made a move first. Other countries then copied that move by making similar laws.

Example 4 — Everyday Life

"At the dinner table, the grandfather bowed his head to pray. Everyone else followed suit."

What it means: The grandfather did something first. Everyone at the table did the same thing in response.
The Key Idea Hidden Inside the Idiom

There is always a sequence implied in this idiom:

  1. Someone acts first. (The "leader" or the one who sets the trend.)
  2. Someone else copies that action. (They "follow suit.")

The person who "follows suit" is almost never the originator of the action. They are the imitator or follower. This is important: the idiom always involves looking at what someone else did and then doing the same.

• It does not mean to follow a person physically (like following someone down the street).
  • It does not mean to agree with someone's opinion — it specifically means copying someone's action.
  • It does not always carry a negative meaning. It is neutral. Sometimes following suit is smart and sensible; other times it might be mindless copying — context decides.
The Tone and Feel of the Idiom

"Follow suit" is a neutral, slightly formal idiom. It sounds natural in:

  • News articles ("The central bank cut interest rates, and commercial banks followed suit.")
  • Business conversations
  • Everyday storytelling
  • Academic writing

It is not slang. It is not rude. It works in both formal and informal settings, though it leans slightly toward formal writing and speech.

❌ "He followed the suit." → Wrong (no "the")
❌ "She followed suits." → Wrong (no plural)
✅ "They followed suit." → Correct

The phrase is always exactly two words: follow suit — nothing added, nothing changed.

"Follow suit" = to do the same thing that someone else has already done.

If you remember just one thing, remember this: it is about copying an action that someone else performed first — just like in a card game, where you must play the same type of card that the first player played.
6281:
To follow through means to complete something fully — not just start it, but see it all the way to the end.

It is the opposite of stopping halfway. When you follow through, you go from the beginning of an action all the way to its natural finish, without quitting, forgetting, or giving up before it is truly done.

Think of it this way: starting something is only half the job. Following through is the other half — the part where you actually finish what you started.
Where the Phrase Comes From (The Physical Origin)

The phrase was born in sports, and understanding its physical meaning makes the figurative meaning much clearer.

Imagine a tennis player hitting a ball. The moment the racket makes contact with the ball is not the end of the swing — the player must continue the full arc of the swing after the ball has left the racket. That continuation of motion is called the follow-through.

The same thing happens in:

  • Golf — the golfer continues swinging the club even after the ball is gone.
  • Baseball/Cricket — the batter or bowler completes their arm motion after releasing the ball.
  • Basketball — a player holds their wrist position even after releasing the ball toward the hoop.

Why does this matter physically? Because stopping the motion too early ruins the shot. The energy and direction you gave the ball come from the entire movement, not just the moment of contact. A player who stops their swing the second they hit the ball produces a weak, inaccurate result.

This is the key insight behind the phrase: what you do after the initial action still matters.

The sports image translated perfectly into everyday life, and that is where most people use it today.

In general life, to follow through means:

  • To do what you said you would do.
  • To complete a task all the way to the end.
  • To not abandon something midway.

It carries an idea of reliability, discipline, and completion.

Simple examples:

  • A manager says, "He always has great ideas, but he never follows through." → He starts things but does not finish them.
  • "She promised to help me, and she followed through." → She actually did what she promised.
  • "You need to follow through on your commitments." → You need to complete the things you have agreed to do.
  • "The government announced the plan but failed to follow through." → They announced it but never actually carried it out.

The phrase can also be used as a noun, usually written with a hyphen: follow-through.

As a noun, it refers to the act of completing something, or to a person's habit or quality of finishing what they start.

Examples:

  • "The project needs better follow-through." → People need to actually complete the tasks, not just talk about them.
  • "Her follow-through is impressive — she always delivers." → She consistently finishes what she starts.
  • "He has no follow-through." → He is unreliable; he does not finish things.

"Follow through" is not just about finishing — it has a specific shade of meaning. It implies that you had already started something, made a plan, or made a promise, and now you are seeing it through to completion.

You would not say, "I followed through by deciding to go to the gym." That is just making a decision.

You would say, "I said I would go to the gym every day this week, and I followed through." That means you actually did it after committing to it.

So the sequence is always: intention or start → then follow-through at the end.

Following through is the bridge between saying and doing, between starting and finishing.

Several other common phrases are closely related:

"Follow through on something" — This is the most common construction. The word on connects the action to a specific thing.
→ "She followed through on her promise."
→ "They didn't follow through on the deal."

"Follow through with something" — Slightly less common but also correct. The word with connects to the method or action.
→ "He followed through with his plan."

"See it through" — A synonym. To see something through means to stay with it until it is finished.
→ "It will be tough, but I'll see it through."

"Go through with something" — Similar, but this one is often used when the situation is difficult or uncomfortable, and you do it anyway.
→ "She was nervous, but she went through with the speech."

"Drop the ball" — The opposite of following through. If you drop the ball, you failed to complete your responsibility.

"Half-hearted" — Describes someone who does not put full effort in and therefore never truly follows through.
Common Contexts Where You Will Hear This

In business:
Leaders speak of following through on strategy, deals, or promises to customers. It is considered a mark of professionalism.

In personal relationships:
Following through on promises builds trust. Not following through — saying you will call, show up, or help, and then not doing it — damages trust and is seen as unreliable behavior.

In sports and fitness:
Both in the literal physical sense (technique) and the figurative sense — committing to a training schedule and actually sticking to it.

In self-development:
A very common piece of advice is that most people fail not because their plans are bad, but because they lack follow-through. The idea: good execution beats good planning without action.

In politics and journalism:
Reporters often ask whether a government or official "followed through" on a campaign promise or announcement.
Why the Concept Matters (The Deeper Idea)

The reason "follow through" is such an important phrase is because human beings are naturally good at starting things — we feel excited, motivated, and full of intention at the beginning. But motivation fades, obstacles appear, and life gets in the way. The people who succeed and the people who are trusted are, very often, simply the ones who finish what they start.

Following through is what separates a wish from an achievement, a promise from a fact, a plan from a result.

FormExample
  • Verb (sports): Continue the motion of your swing or throw past the point of contact.
  • Verb (general): Complete what you started; do what you promised.
  • Noun: The quality or act of completing things — "She has great follow-through."
  • Key prepositions: *follow through on a promise / *follow through with a plan.
  • Opposite of: Quitting, abandoning, forgetting, dropping the ball.
  • Associated with: Reliability, discipline, trustworthiness, and success.

In one sentence: "Follow through" means to finish what you started and do what you said you would do — all the way to the end, without stopping short.
6282: At its most essential level, a follower is someone who comes after, goes behind, or orients themselves according to another person, idea, or force. The word always implies a relationship — there is always something or someone being followed.

1. A person who accepts the beliefs, teachings, or leadership of someone or something

This is the oldest and most important meaning of the word. When you believe in someone's ideas, support their cause, or shape your life according to their guidance, you are their follower.

The key idea is voluntary alignment — a follower looks up to someone and consciously chooses to go in the direction that person or belief system points them toward.

Examples:

  • "He was a lifelong follower of Gandhi." (He believed in Gandhi's principles and tried to live by them.)
  • "She became a follower of Buddhism after years of searching." (She adopted Buddhist teachings as her guiding philosophy.)
  • "The philosopher had many followers who spread his ideas across Europe."

In religious contexts, this meaning runs especially deep. The followers of Jesus, the followers of the Prophet Muhammad, the followers of the Buddha — these are people whose entire worldview and way of life is shaped by devotion to those figures' teachings. The word in this context carries a strong sense of commitment, loyalty, and personal transformation.

In political contexts, a follower of a leader or a movement is someone who supports and acts in accordance with that leader's vision — a loyal supporter, not just a passive observer.

2. A person who subscribes to someone's content on social media

In the age of the internet, this meaning has become extremely common — possibly the most frequently heard use of the word today.

When you click "Follow" on someone's Instagram, YouTube, X (formerly Twitter), or any similar platform, you become their follower. This means their posts, videos, or updates will appear in your feed automatically.

Examples:

  • "The influencer gained ten million followers in a year."
  • "She checked her follower count every morning."
  • "He followed the account but wasn't a very engaged follower — he rarely watched their videos."

In this modern sense, the relationship can range from deeply engaged (someone who watches every video, buys every product, feels a personal connection) to completely passive (someone who followed once and never looks at the content again). The word itself doesn't tell you which — context does.

An important nuance: unlike the religious or philosophical meaning above, being a social media follower carries no expectation of personal commitment or belief. It is often a very light relationship.

3. A person who conforms to others rather than thinking or leading independently

This is a more evaluative use of the word — it describes someone who lacks the initiative or courage to form their own views and instead does what the people around them do, what's trendy, or what authority figures tell them.

This meaning almost always carries a slightly critical or negative tone. It's used to say that someone is passive, impressionable, or unoriginal.

Examples:

  • "She always does what her friends do. She's a follower, not a leader."
  • "Don't just be a follower — form your own opinion."
  • "The company didn't innovate; it was always a follower of whatever competitors were doing."

The natural contrast here is with a leader — someone who sets direction, thinks independently, and takes initiative. In this context, follower suggests the person is reactive, not proactive.

4. A person who physically comes after someone (in a line, march, or procession)

This is the most literal meaning and the least common in modern everyday speech. It simply describes someone who is walking or moving behind another person.

Example:

  • "The king walked into the hall, and his followers entered behind him."

In historical writing, you'll often see this sense — an army commander's followers, a queen's followers — meaning those who literally marched or travelled with them.

Follower vs. fan: A fan is someone who admires a person (a celebrity, an athlete) with enthusiasm, often without any ideological alignment. A follower implies a closer, more committed relationship — you follow someone's ideas or direction, not just admire them from a distance. In social media, however, the two words blur considerably.

Follower vs. disciple: A disciple is essentially a deeper, more intimate version of a follower. A disciple is personally taught by a teacher, is close to them, and carries their teachings forward with dedication. A follower can be distant — someone who only reads about a person's ideas without ever meeting them. All disciples are followers, but not all followers are disciples.

Follower vs. supporter: A supporter backs someone but doesn't necessarily shape their life around that person's ideas. A follower is more aligned, more committed. You can support a political candidate while remaining somewhat detached; a follower is more deeply invested.

The word follower is essentially neutral on its own, but the context it appears in gives it one of three tones:

Positive or admiring: "She was a devoted follower of the Stoic philosophers and lived with extraordinary discipline." Here, being a follower is a mark of wisdom and commitment.

Neutral and descriptive: "The celebrity's followers were notified of the new post instantly." No judgment — simply a technical fact about social media.

Critical or dismissive: "He doesn't have an original thought. He's just a follower." Here the word implies weakness, lack of independent thought, or passivity.

Blind follower: Someone who follows without any questioning, critical thinking, or independent judgment. This is always used critically. "A blind follower of the cult leader, he accepted every instruction without doubt."

Follower count: The total number of people who follow someone on a social media platform. "Her follower count jumped from a thousand to a million overnight after the video went viral."

True follower / devoted follower: Emphasizes deep commitment and sincerity. "Only a true follower of the teaching would have the patience to practice it for decades."
The Relationship Between Follower and Leader

The word follower only truly makes full sense when you understand it in relation to its natural counterpart: the leader. In virtually every human system — religion, politics, social movements, organizations, online communities — there is at least one leader and many followers.

This leader-follower dynamic is not inherently one of inequality or weakness. In many traditions, being a sincere, thoughtful follower of a wise teacher is considered one of the noblest things a person can do. The word becomes negative only when following is done blindly, without thought, or simply to avoid the discomfort of thinking for oneself.

In a completely separate, technical domain, a follower (more precisely, a cam follower) is a mechanical component. It presses against a rotating or sliding part called a cam and physically "follows" the cam's shape, converting one type of motion into another. You would encounter this only in engineering or mechanical contexts — it has nothing to do with the human and social meanings above.

SenseWhat it meansTone

A follower is someone who aligns themselves with another. In its deepest sense, it is a person who accepts the beliefs or leadership of another. In its modern everyday sense, it is most commonly a social media subscriber. In its critical sense, it describes someone who lacks the independence to lead or think for themselves. And in its most literal sense, it is simply someone who comes after another physically. The right meaning in any given sentence is always determined by context — once you have these four senses clear in your mind, you will always be able to identify which one is at work.
6283:
Folly means serious foolishness — the kind that comes from a lack of wisdom, judgment, or good sense. It's not just a small slip or honest mistake. Folly is what happens when someone acts in a way that is obviously unwise, reckless, or impractical — and often suffers the consequences for it.

Think of it this way: if you forget to buy milk, that's a mistake. But if you spend your entire life savings on a business idea that any sensible person could see would fail, that's folly.

"Folly" works in two distinct ways, and it's important to understand both.

1. Folly as a quality or state of mind

Here, folly refers to the general condition of being foolish — a pattern of poor judgment or unwise thinking. It's often used to describe the foolishness of a person, a group, or even all of humanity.

  • "The folly of the king's decision led to the destruction of his kingdom."
  • "History is full of human folly."

In this sense, it's almost like a character flaw, not just one bad moment.

2. Folly as a specific foolish action or plan

Here, folly refers to one particular act or decision that is wildly unwise or impractical. The plural in this sense is follies.

  • "Buying a boat he couldn't afford was just one of his many follies."
  • "Starting a war on two fronts was a monumental folly."

Folly sits on the stronger end of the foolishness scale. Here's a simple way to picture the scale:

Mistake → Blunder → Foolishness → Folly → Madness

A "mistake" is neutral — anyone can make one. "Folly" carries a sense of judgment: it suggests the person should have known better, or that the foolishness was obvious to everyone around them, even if not to the person committing it. It also implies that real consequences follow — folly usually isn't harmless.

Folly is a somewhat formal and literary word. You'll see it more in books, speeches, editorials, and serious writing than in everyday casual conversation. When someone uses it, it often carries a tone of wisdom looking back at stupidity — like a wise elder shaking their head at poor decisions.

It's also a timeless word. Writers use it to talk about the foolishness of ancient rulers, modern politicians, or ordinary people alike. This makes it a powerful word when you want to sound measured and thoughtful rather than just saying "that was so dumb."
A Completely Different Meaning: The Architectural Folly

This one surprises most learners: the word "folly" has an entirely separate meaning in architecture.

An architectural folly is a building — often ornate and elaborate — that was built purely for decoration and serves no practical purpose whatsoever. These were popular among wealthy landowners in 18th and 19th century England, who would build fake ruins, miniature castles, eccentric towers, fake Gothic churches, or artificial grottos on their large estates, purely to make the landscape look romantic, dramatic, or interesting.

Why are they called follies? Because building something expensive and elaborate that does nothing useful was seen as the ultimate act of whimsical foolishness — only the very rich could afford such pointless extravagance. The name stuck.

Today, the term is sometimes extended to describe any ambitious project that turns out to be pointless, impractical, or a waste of resources — even outside architecture. For example, a massively expensive government project that achieves nothing might be called "an expensive folly."
A Third Use: Follies (as a show)

In the world of entertainment, Follies (almost always plural, and often capitalized) refers to a type of lavish, elaborate stage show or revue — typically featuring music, glamour, and spectacle. The most famous example is the Ziegfeld Follies, a series of spectacular Broadway shows from the early 20th century. The name playfully nods at the idea of extravagant, over-the-top entertainment — expensive and dazzling, much like the architectural follies.

• "The folly of youth" — the foolish decisions young people make because they lack experience.
  • "It would be sheer folly to..." — it would be absolutely unwise to do something.
  • "The follies of mankind" — the many foolish patterns repeated throughout human history.
  • "A costly folly" — a foolish decision that came with a heavy price.

MeaningWhat it means
State of foolishnessA general lack of wisdom or good judgment
A foolish actA specific unwise decision or course of action
Architectural follyA decorative, purposeless building
Follies (entertainment)A lavish, spectacular stage revue

The word "folly" is ultimately about the gap between what wisdom demands and what was actually done — and the consequences that fill that gap. Whether it's a bad decision, a useless tower in a garden, or the grand foolishness of history's great blunders, folly always points to that same human tendency to act without adequate sense or foresight.
6284:
To foment means to deliberately stir up, encourage, or keep alive something negative — most often unrest, conflict, hatred, or rebellion — usually in a slow, sustained, and somewhat secretive way.

You are not the one directly causing the chaos. You are the one quietly feeding it, nudging it forward, and helping it grow in others.

Think of someone who keeps whispering poisonous things about a colleague to their coworkers — not starting a fight directly, but slowly planting seeds of resentment, week after week, until the workplace is in turmoil. That person is fomenting conflict.

Or picture a foreign government secretly funding extremist groups in a rival country, spreading propaganda, and exploiting existing grievances — not openly invading, but gradually stirring the population toward civil unrest. That government is fomenting rebellion.

The key image is this: not a single explosive spark, but a slow, deliberate fanning of embers over time.
What kinds of things get fomented

"Foment" almost always pairs with something negative. You will most commonly see it used with words like rebellion, revolution, unrest, discord, conflict, tension, hatred, dissent, violence, and trouble. You almost never foment something good. If you see the word, expect something dark or destructive nearby.

There are three things that make "foment" distinct and precise:

It is always deliberate. You cannot accidentally foment something. There is always intent behind it — someone is consciously working to stir things up.

It is usually covert or indirect. The person fomenting trouble is often working behind the scenes. They are not standing at the front of the riot — they are the ones who stirred the crowd up before slipping away.

It implies a process, not a moment. Fomenting something takes time. It is a sustained effort — encouraging, nurturing, and keeping something destructive alive and growing.
How it compares to similar words

These words overlap with "foment" but are not the same:

Incite is more immediate and direct — you incite a crowd to riot right now, in the moment, often openly. Foment is slower and more behind-the-scenes.

Provoke means to trigger a reaction, often through a direct action or insult. It can be unintentional. Foment is always deliberate and more gradual.

Instigate means to initiate or set something in motion. It focuses on the starting point. Foment focuses more on the sustained encouragement of something already simmering.

If "incite" is striking a match, "foment" is quietly keeping the fire fed over weeks.

"The radical newspaper was accused of fomenting class hatred by publishing inflammatory articles every day."

"Rival politicians fomented resentment among rural voters by constantly blaming the urban elite for their problems."

"The intelligence report concluded that the foreign power had spent years fomenting unrest in the region before the uprising finally broke out."

"He wasn't the one throwing punches — but he had spent months fomenting the tension that led to the fight."

"The speech was seen as an attempt to foment division within the party at a critical moment."
Where you will encounter this word

"Foment" is a formal word. You will encounter it most in journalism, political commentary, history books, legal documents, and academic writing. You would not use it in casual conversation ("he fomented drama at the party" would sound odd). It lives in serious, often weighty contexts — discussions of political movements, wars, propaganda, social unrest, and power.

Use "foment" when you want to convey that someone is deliberately and methodically stirring up something destructive — not loudly and directly, but quietly and persistently, often from behind the scenes. The word carries a sense of cunning and calculated intent. When you write or say it, your reader immediately understands: this was not an accident. Someone worked to make this happen.
6285:
"Fond of" means to have a warm, gentle, and deep liking for something or someone. When you are fond of something, you don't just casually like it — you have a soft, affectionate feeling toward it that has settled comfortably in your heart.

Think of it this way:

You don't just notice it. You enjoy it. You care about it. It makes you feel good.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

"Fond" is an adjective. On its own, it means "having a liking or affection for something." But here's the important rule: "fond" almost never stands alone. It almost always needs the word "of" right after it to be complete and make proper sense.

"Of" is a preposition here. It connects the feeling (fond) to its target — the thing or person you like.

So the structure is always:

Someone + is/was/am/are + fond of + [the thing or person they like]

This is crucial to understand. In English, liking something exists on a scale:

Like → Fond of → Love

  • "I like pizza" — simple, neutral, no strong emotion.
  • "I am fond of pizza" — warmer, more personal. There's a genuine affection here. It's been part of your life; it brings you comfort or joy.
  • "I love pizza" — the strongest form of liking.

So "fond of" sits in the middle zone — it is stronger and warmer than a plain "like," but not as intense as "love." It carries a feeling of tenderness, comfort, and genuine affection.

You can be fond of almost anything:

1. A person

"She is very fond of her grandfather."

(She has deep warmth and affection for him.)

2. An animal or pet

"The children are fond of the stray cat in the neighborhood."

(They care for it genuinely.)

3. A food or drink

"He is particularly fond of dark chocolate."

(He doesn't just eat it — he enjoys it with real pleasure.)

4. An activity (using verb + -ing)

"My mother is fond of gardening."

(She finds real joy and comfort in it.)

5. A place

"I have always been fond of this little town."

(It holds a warm place in my heart.)

6. A subject or idea

"She is fond of history."

(She genuinely enjoys and appreciates it.)
The Grammar Rule You Must Remember

After "fond," always use "of." Never use "for," "with," "about," or any other preposition.

✅ Correct: "He is fond of classical music."
❌ Wrong: "He is fond for classical music."
❌ Wrong: "He is fond with classical music."

Also, when the thing you are fond of is an action, you must use the -ing form of the verb (called a gerund):

✅ "She is fond of reading."
✅ "He is fond of swimming."
❌ "She is fond of read."
"Grow Fond of" — A Very Important Variation

One of the most common and beautiful uses of this idiom is "grow fond of" or "become fond of." This means that the affection did not exist at the beginning — it developed slowly over time.

"At first, he didn't enjoy classical music, but over the years, he grew fond of it."

"She didn't like her new city at first, but she became fond of it after a few months."

This phrase captures something very real about human experience — how we sometimes slowly fall into liking something the more time we spend with it.

This is something many learners miss, and it is important. "Fond of" carries a slightly nostalgic, tender, and sometimes old-fashioned warmth. It feels more personal and more heartfelt than just saying "I like."

Compare these two sentences:

  • "I like my old neighborhood." (neutral, factual)
  • "I am fond of my old neighborhood." (warm, personal, slightly nostalgic — it means something to you)

When you say you are fond of someone or something, you are communicating not just a preference, but a soft emotional bond.

"Fond of" works in both formal and informal contexts, but it carries a slightly literary and refined quality. You might find it more often in books, letters, or thoughtful conversation than in very casual slang-heavy speech. That said, it is completely natural to use it in everyday conversation:

"I'm quite fond of that café on the corner."
"He's always been fond of telling long stories."

Here are the most useful patterns for you to practice:

  • "I am fond of _." → I am fond of jazz music.
  • "She/He is fond of _." → She is fond of her students.
  • "They are very fond of _." → They are very fond of hiking.
  • "I have always been fond of _." → I have always been fond of old movies.
  • "I grew fond of _ over time." → I grew fond of the rainy weather over time.
  • "He/She is particularly fond of _." → He is particularly fond of spicy food.

QuestionAnswer

"Fond of" means to have a warm, affectionate, and genuine liking for someone or something. It is stronger than a plain "like" but not as intense as "love." It always uses the preposition "of" — never anything else. It can be used with people, things, places, and activities (using the -ing form for activities). The phrase "grow fond of" means to gradually develop this warm feeling over time. The overall emotional tone is tender, personal, and slightly nostalgic.

Once you understand "fond of," you will start noticing it everywhere — in books, conversations, and everyday speech — and you will recognize exactly the soft, warm layer of emotion it carries each time it appears.
6286: Fontina (noun) is a type of cheese — specifically, a semi-soft to semi-hard cow's milk cheese that originated in the Aosta Valley, a small mountainous region in northwestern Italy near the Alps.

A wheel of fontina has a thin, brownish-orange outer rind. On the inside, the cheese is pale ivory or pale yellow in color, smooth in texture, and dotted with small, irregular holes (called "eyes"). When young, it feels soft and slightly springy. As it ages, it becomes firmer and drier.

Fontina has a flavor that is mild, buttery, and nutty — with a gentle earthiness underneath. It is not sharp or pungent. Think of it as rich and creamy, but not overpowering. The longer it is aged, the more complex and slightly stronger the flavor becomes. Authentic Italian fontina often carries a faint mushroom-like or grassy note, which comes from the milk of cows that graze on Alpine meadow grass.
Why it is special in cooking

The most celebrated quality of fontina is how it melts. It melts smoothly and evenly, without becoming greasy or stringy. This makes it one of the most prized cheeses for cooking. It is the traditional cheese used in fonduta, which is the Italian version of fondue — a warm, creamy cheese dip often enriched with egg yolks and truffles. Beyond fonduta, fontina is widely used in:

  • Pasta dishes — stirred into sauces for a silky, creamy finish
  • Pizzas and flatbreads — for a smooth, golden melt
  • Grilled sandwiches and panini — it melts into the bread beautifully
  • Risottos and polenta — folded in at the end to add creaminess
  • Gratins and casseroles — baked on top to form a golden crust
  • Cheese boards — served alongside fruits, nuts, and cured meats

This is an important distinction. True, authentic fontina is called Fontina Val d'Aosta and carries a protected designation of origin (a certification that guarantees it was made in the Aosta Valley using traditional methods and local milk). This is the version prized by chefs and food lovers.

However, because the name "fontina" became popular worldwide, many other countries — including Denmark, Sweden, and the United States — began making their own versions. These imitations are typically milder, softer, more rubbery, and much less complex in flavor than the real Italian fontina. They melt reasonably well but lack the depth, earthiness, and nuttiness of the authentic cheese. You can often spot the imitations on a grocery shelf by their bright red wax coating, which the genuine Italian product does not have.
How it is made (in simple terms)

Authentic fontina is made from raw, unpasteurized whole milk from Valdostana cows — a breed native to the Aosta Valley. The milk is collected once a day, and cheesemaking begins almost immediately while the milk is still fresh and warm. After the cheese is formed and pressed into wheels, it is aged in cool, humid Alpine caves or cellars for a minimum of 80 days, during which time the wheels are regularly turned, salted, and brushed. This careful aging process is what gives it its distinctive flavor and texture.
How it fits into the broader world of cheese

If you already know certain cheeses, fontina sits comfortably in the same family as Gruyère, Gouda, and Havarti — all of which are semi-hard, cow's milk cheeses with good melting qualities and mild-to-nutty flavors. Fontina is not as sharp as aged Gruyère, not as sweet as Gouda, and not as plain as Havarti. It occupies a unique middle ground that is earthy and deeply savory.

Fontina is a smooth, nutty, mildly earthy Italian cheese made from cow's milk, beloved above all for its exceptional melting ability. The authentic version comes from the Aosta Valley in Italy and is a highly regarded, carefully protected product. Cheaper imitations exist worldwide and are widely available, but they are noticeably blander. Whether melted into a sauce, baked over a dish, or simply eaten on its own, fontina is considered one of Italy's finest cheeses.
6287:
A food court is a large, open area — usually inside a shopping mall, airport, or similar building — where many different food stalls or small restaurants are grouped together in one place, and all of them share a single common dining area with tables and chairs where customers sit and eat.

Think of it like this: instead of one big restaurant run by one owner serving one type of food, a food court is like many small restaurants sitting side by side under the same roof, each serving different kinds of food, and all sharing the same eating space.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

"Food" — obviously refers to things you eat and drink.

"Court" — in architecture, a "court" means an open, central space that is surrounded by other structures. Like a courtyard in a palace or a castle, a food court is a central open space surrounded by food stalls on the sides.

Put them together: a food court = a central open space for eating, surrounded by multiple food vendors.
What Does a Food Court Look Like?

When you walk into a food court, here is what you typically see:

Around the edges or along the walls, you will find individual food stalls or counters. Each stall belongs to a different brand or vendor. One might sell burgers, another pizza, another Chinese noodles, another tacos, another fried chicken, another ice cream, and so on. Each stall has its own menu, its own kitchen, its own staff, and its own cash counter where you pay and place your order.

In the middle (or centre) of the space, you will find a large shared seating area filled with tables and chairs. This is where all the customers — regardless of which stall they ordered from — sit down and eat. A person eating a burger from Stall A and a person eating sushi from Stall B will both be sitting in the same shared seating area. Nobody "owns" a particular table — it is first come, first served.
How Does It Work? (Step by Step)

1. You walk into the food court and look around at all the available stalls.
  2. You choose which stall you want to order from (based on what food you feel like eating).
  3. You walk up to that stall's counter, look at its menu (usually displayed on a board above), and place your order.
  4. You pay at that stall's counter.
  5. You either wait briefly at the counter while your food is prepared, or you take a number/buzzer and find a seat while waiting.
  6. Once you have your food (usually served on a tray), you take it to any available table in the shared seating area and eat.
  7. When you are done, you typically clean up after yourself by disposing of your trash in nearby bins and returning your tray to a designated spot (though in some countries, staff may do this for you).
Where Are Food Courts Found?

Food courts are most commonly found in:

Shopping Malls — This is the most classic location. Almost every large mall in the world has a food court, usually on one of its floors (often the top floor or basement level). Shoppers can take a break from shopping, grab a meal, and then continue.

Airports — Airports have food courts so that travellers can eat quickly between flights without having to sit down at a full-service restaurant and wait a long time.

University and College Campuses — Many universities have food courts in their student centres so students can choose from a variety of food options during lunch breaks.

Office Buildings and Business Complexes — Large office parks sometimes have food courts in their ground floors or attached buildings so that office workers can grab quick lunches.

Hospitals — Large hospitals sometimes have food courts so patients' families, visitors, and hospital staff can access diverse food options conveniently.

Amusement Parks and Sports Stadiums — These large venues often have food court-style areas to serve large crowds quickly.

Train Stations and Bus Terminals — Similar to airports, these transit hubs often have food courts for commuters on the go.
The History of Food Courts

The food court as we know it today did not always exist. It is a relatively modern invention.

The concept originated in the United States in the 1970s. The first widely recognised food court appeared at the Paramus Park Mall in New Jersey and the Plymouth Meeting Mall in Pennsylvania, both in 1974. Mall developers noticed that people were spending a lot of time in malls and needed a place to eat, but a single large restaurant could not serve the enormous variety of tastes people had. Their solution: bring together many different food vendors under one roof, in one open space.
